newsitem.title: USA: Terrorism said rising, with religion in a major role.
newsitem.headline: Terrorism said rising, with religion in a major role.

text.p: Terrorism is increasing in intensity, with religion a motivating force, a meeting on aviation safety and security was told on Tuesday.

Bruce Hoffman, director of the Centre for Terrorism and Political Violence at St Andrews University, Scotland, said that "although the total volume of terrorist incidents world-wide has declined in the 1990s, the proportion of persons killed in terrorist incidents has steadily risen."

His remarks were made at a conference sponsored by George Washington University and the White House Commission on Aviation Safety and Security, formed after the TWA crash off Long Island, New York, last July that killed all 230 people on board.
Investigators are pursuing three main theories for what caused the crash -- a bomb, missile or mechanical failure.

Hoffman said the rise in deaths from terrorism incidents was due to the increase in the number of religious extremist groups, the proliferation of "amateurs" who can easily acquire weapons and the increasing competence of "professional" terrorists.
He said that while attacks on civil aviation are relatively rare, officials responsible for protecting aviation face a daunting task in deciding what level of protection to put into place.
The White House commission has called for increased airport security measures, including the use of advanced x-ray baggage screening.

General Shlomo Gazit, former chief of Israeli military intelligence, said the threat of attacks against civil aviation cannot be separated from terrorism in general and from state support of terrorism.

He said the bombing of planes, for instance, increasingly needs state support for financing and training and he said he was necessary to stay vigilant to ensure that no state helped extremists acquire nuclear weapons.

"The probability of the use of nuclear weapons by terrorists has significantly increased in the last decade," Gazit said, due to the disintegrating Soviet Union's weakened control over existing weapons.
Gazit said extremist religious groups could use weapons not only for blackmail but also for punishment.

"Such organisations are not bound by normal rational considerations, and if they may decide to use such weapons, it will not be in order to make publicity for their cause but for pure punishment," Gazit said.
